Taylor's Theorem: The Remainder Envelope

This scene shows the band that traps the Taylor error. Raise the degree and the band shrinks to zero.

The remainder has a ceiling. So you can promise in advance how large the error can get. The true curve always stays inside the band.

For example, measuring with a 📏 ruler promises an error of at most a millimeter. The Taylor remainder makes the same kind of promise. Higher degree narrows the promised range.

f(x)=Tn(x)+Rn(x),∣Rn(x)∣≤∣x∣n+1(n+1)!f(x) = T_n(x) + R_n(x), \quad |R_n(x)| \le \frac{|x|^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}f(x)=Tn​(x)+Rn​(x),∣Rn​(x)∣≤(n+1)!∣x∣n+1​

If f(x)=∑k=0∞ck(x−a)kf(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} c_k (x-a)^kf(x)=∑k=0∞​ck​(x−a)k can be differentiated termwise, prove ck=f(k)(a)k!c_k = \frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k!}ck​=k!f(k)(a)​ (uniqueness of Taylor coefficients).

f(x)=∑k=0∞ck(x−a)k  ⇒  cj=f(j)(a)j!f(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} c_k (x-a)^k \;\Rightarrow\; c_j = \frac{f^{(j)}(a)}{j!}f(x)=k=0∑∞​ck​(x−a)k⇒cj​=j!f(j)(a)​
Show proof

  1. Assume f(x)=∑k=0∞ck(x−a)kf(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} c_k (x-a)^kf(x)=∑k=0∞​ck​(x−a)k converges near aaa. By the power series theorem, a power series is termwise differentiable to all orders inside its radius of convergence, so the repeated termwise differentiation used below (differentiating jjj times for arbitrary jjj) is justified — this theorem is cited here to align the hypotheses.

  2. Differentiating jjj times gives f(j)(x)=∑k=j∞k(k−1)⋯(k−j+1) ck (x−a)k−jf^{(j)}(x) = \sum_{k=j}^{\infty} k(k-1)\cdots(k-j+1)\,c_k\,(x-a)^{k-j}f(j)(x)=∑k=j∞​k(k−1)⋯(k−j+1)ck​(x−a)k−j (terms with k<jk < jk<j vanish in the differentiation).

  3. Setting x=ax = ax=a kills every term with k>jk > jk>j via (x−a)k−j(x-a)^{k-j}(x−a)k−j; only k=jk = jk=j survives, giving f(j)(a)=j! cjf^{(j)}(a) = j!\,c_jf(j)(a)=j!cj​, i.e. cj=f(j)(a)j!c_j = \frac{f^{(j)}(a)}{j!}cj​=j!f(j)(a)​ — the Taylor coefficients are unique.
